families.name: Feature Attribution
families.definition: Methods that assign importance scores to individual input features to explain specific model predictions.

properties.text: These methods typically compute gradients or perturbations to quantify the influence of each feature on the output.
They provide local explanations for single instances rather than global model behavior.
Common techniques include LIME, SHAP, and Integrated Gradients.
They are model-agnostic and can be applied to any differentiable or black-box model.
They help identify which parts of an image or text contributed most to a classification decision.

limitations.text: Attribution scores can be unstable and sensitive to small input perturbations.
They often fail to capture higher-order interactions between features.
The choice of baseline or background distribution significantly affects the resulting attributions.
They do not guarantee that the identified features are causally responsible for the prediction.
Computational cost can be high for high-dimensional inputs requiring many perturbation samples.

families.name: Activation Visualization
families.definition: Techniques that visualize internal neuron activations or feature maps to understand what the network has learned.

properties.text: These methods display heatmaps of activation values across layers to reveal spatial or temporal patterns.
They allow researchers to inspect intermediate representations without modifying the model architecture.
Common approaches include visualizing convolutional filters and ReLU activations.
They provide insight into the hierarchical structure of learned features.
They are particularly useful for understanding computer vision models.

limitations.text: Visualizations can be misleading if not interpreted with knowledge of the specific layer's role.
They do not directly explain the final prediction but only show internal states.
High-dimensional activations are difficult to interpret visually without dimensionality reduction.
They may highlight artifacts or noise rather than meaningful semantic features.
They are less applicable to non-spatial data types like tabular data or text.

families.name: Model Simplification
families.definition: Approaches that replace complex deep networks with simpler, more interpretable surrogate models.

properties.text: These methods fit a transparent model, such as a decision tree or linear regression, to mimic the behavior of the deep network.
They aim to provide global explanations by capturing the overall decision boundary.
Common techniques include distillation and fitting generalized additive models.
They allow for easier analysis of the model's general logic and rules.
They can be used to detect biases or unfairness in the original model's decisions.

limitations.text: Surrogate models may not accurately capture the complex, non-linear relationships of the original network.
The fidelity of the surrogate depends heavily on the choice of the simpler model class.
They may fail to explain specific edge cases or local behaviors of the deep model.
The process of fitting the surrogate can be computationally expensive for large datasets.
There is no guarantee that the simplified model reflects the true causal mechanisms of the original model.

families.name: Causal Analysis
families.definition: Methods that use causal inference frameworks to determine the causal relationship between inputs and outputs.

properties.text: These approaches distinguish between correlation and causation in the model's decision-making process.
They often involve interventions or counterfactual reasoning to test the necessity and sufficiency of features.
Common techniques include causal graphs and do-calculus applied to neural networks.
They provide a more rigorous foundation for understanding model behavior than correlation-based methods.
They can help identify spurious correlations that the model may have learned.

limitations.text: Causal assumptions are often difficult to verify or justify in real-world scenarios.
The computational complexity of causal inference can be prohibitive for large models.
They require strong assumptions about the underlying data-generating process.
They are less mature and less widely adopted than feature attribution methods.
They may not scale well to high-dimensional inputs with complex dependencies.
Lack of a unified theoretical framework that connects different interpretation methods.
Difficulty in evaluating the quality and faithfulness of explanations objectively.
Scalability of interpretation methods to very large and complex models.
Ensuring that explanations are robust to adversarial attacks and distribution shifts.
Bridging the gap between local explanations and global model understanding.
Developing standardized benchmarks for comparing different interpretation techniques.
Understanding how interpretation methods perform on non-vision tasks like NLP and tabular data.
Integrating interpretability into the model training process rather than post-hoc analysis.
